papers.summary: Urban Beauty asks a deceptively simple question: what does it mean to make cities beautiful? Most of us agree that beautiful streets, buildings, and public spaces enrich our lives. They lift spirits, strengthen communities, and even improve health. Yet the moment we try to define ‘urban beauty’, certainty crumbles. Is beauty objective, something we ‘know when we see it’? Or is it wholly subjective, forever ‘in the eye of the beholder’? This book explores the fertile tension between these poles. Around the world, governments now regulate for beauty, planners and designers are tasked with delivering it, and communities increasingly demand it. But how do we pursue something that resists clear definition? papers.summary: Treating novel and film as thesis and antithesis, this chapter draws out ideas about breath in the novel and explores their transfer to the screen. It therefore seeks evidence of synthesis in how Zhao elicits meaning from camera movement and editing, choral music and breathing sounds, and a juxtaposition of close-ups with deep-focus wide and long shots that both simulates and stimulates breathing. Consequently, this analysis reinforces the theme of interconnectedness by consideration of the adaptation process as an exchange of energy between the novel and the film, by tracking descriptions of breathing in the novel and following this by analysing corresponding scenes in the film. Finally, this chapter explores how the link between ancient Daoist traditions of meditation and universal experiences of grief provides evidence of Zhao as an atemporal, transnational, peripatetic filmmaker.

papers.summary: With the emergence of technologies for collecting data for the body, such as motion tracking and biosignal sensing, there has been an interest in using these technologies in performing arts. In such performance settings, this data has been mapped to different types of output, such as audio-visuals. In this chapter, we discuss the intersection of embodied interaction, performing arts and audio-visual practice. In particular, we will present two lines of work, one exploring audio-visuals in contemporary dance (the Moving Digits project) and another combining gesture, electronic music, and visuals (works by Atau Tanaka).
